blocks.text: After a brainstem stroke, a 66-year-old man coughs and gurgles after every sip of water. His tongue moves, his lips close, and the first part of the swallow looks normal, but the second part, which should seal the airway in a fraction of a second, is failing. A swallow is a reflex with a strict sequence, and each step has its muscles and nerves.

blocks.markdown:
**Swallowing (deglutition)** moves food from the mouth to the stomach while protecting the airway. It has three stages.

1. **Oral stage (voluntary).** The food bolus is chewed (muscles of mastication, **mandibular nerve V3**), formed by the tongue (**hypoglossal nerve XII**), and pushed back against the hard palate to the oropharynx. Mylohyoid (V3) and geniohyoid (C1 fibres running with XII) help raise the floor of the mouth and hyoid.
2. **Pharyngeal stage (involuntary reflex, about 1 second).** Triggered by the bolus touching the oropharynx (afferent: **glossopharyngeal IX**, with vagus X), integrated by a swallowing centre in the **medulla**. The **soft palate rises** (levator veli palatini, via the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus; tensor veli palatini by V3) to seal the nasopharynx; the **larynx and hyoid are elevated** and the **epiglottis tilts** back over the laryngeal inlet while the vocal cords adduct; the **pharyngeal constrictors** (vagus, pharyngeal plexus) contract in sequence, and the **upper oesophageal sphincter** (cricopharyngeus) relaxes. Stylopharyngeus (IX) elevates the pharynx. Breathing is briefly inhibited.
3. **Oesophageal stage (involuntary).** **Peristalsis**, controlled by the vagus and the enteric nervous system, carries the bolus to the stomach.

rows: Soft palate (X, V3), constrictors (X), stylopharyngeus (IX); afferents IX and X
Striated then smooth muscle of oesophagus (X, enteric plexus)

blocks.title: Why food does not enter the nose or the airway
blocks.prompt: List the events in the pharyngeal stage that prevent food entering the nasal cavity and the larynx.

steps.text: Nasal protection: the soft palate is elevated (levator veli palatini, tensor veli palatini) and meets the posterior pharyngeal wall, closing the nasopharynx.
Laryngeal protection: the larynx is pulled up and forward under the tongue base, the epiglottis tilts over the inlet, and the vocal cords and vestibular folds adduct.
Propulsion: the constrictors contract from superior to inferior and the cricopharyngeus relaxes, directing the bolus into the oesophagus.

blocks.answer: Palatal elevation seals the nasopharynx; laryngeal elevation, epiglottic tilt and vocal cord adduction seal the airway; sequential constriction drives the bolus down.

blocks.markdown:
**The larynx.** The larynx is formed by nine cartilages. The three large unpaired ones are the **thyroid cartilage** (the largest; its laminae meet in the laryngeal prominence), the **cricoid cartilage** (the only complete ring, at the lower end) and the **epiglottis** (elastic cartilage). The paired cartilages are the **arytenoids** (which rotate and slide on the cricoid and carry the vocal processes), the **corniculate** and the **cuneiform** cartilages. The **vocal folds** run from the thyroid cartilage in front to the arytenoids behind; the gap between them is the **rima glottidis**.

**Intrinsic muscles** change the tension and position of the vocal folds:
- **Posterior cricoarytenoid**: the only muscle that **abducts** (opens) the vocal folds.
- **Lateral cricoarytenoid** and **transverse/oblique arytenoids**: **adduct** the folds (closing the glottis).
- **Thyroarytenoid** (with **vocalis**): relaxes and shortens the folds.
- **Cricothyroid**: tenses and lengthens the folds, raising pitch.

**Nerve supply.** All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the **recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN)**, a branch of the vagus, **except cricothyroid**, supplied by the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**. Sensation above the folds is by the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; below the folds by the RLN.

**The recurrent laryngeal nerve.** The RLNs ascend in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus to the larynx. On the **right** the nerve loops under the **right subclavian artery**; on the **left** it loops under the **arch of the aorta** (beside the ligamentum arteriosum), so it has a longer course in the chest. Each lies close to the **thyroid gland**, and is vulnerable in thyroid surgery, to tumours at the lung apex or mediastinum, and to an enlarged left atrium or aortic aneurysm on the left.

**Consequences of injury.** **Unilateral RLN palsy**: the affected vocal fold is paralysed (usually near the midline), the voice becomes **hoarse and breathy** and weak, and cough is weak, but airway is usually adequate. **Bilateral RLN palsy**: both folds lie close to the midline, causing **stridor** and airway obstruction. Injury to the external laryngeal nerve (cricothyroid) causes a monotonous voice with loss of high pitch.

blocks.title: Hoarseness from a mediastinal mass
blocks.prompt: A 65-year-old smoker has a hoarse voice. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal fold paralysed near the midline. Chest imaging is requested. Explain why the chest is examined.

steps.text: The left RLN supplies all intrinsic muscles on the left except cricothyroid, so paralysis of the left fold points to the left RLN or vagus.
The left RLN loops around the aortic arch in the thorax, so a lesion in the mediastinum, aortic arch or left lung apex can compress it.
Imaging of the chest therefore looks for a tumour, nodal mass or aneurysm along this course.

blocks.answer: The long thoracic course of the left RLN means a left vocal fold palsy can result from a chest lesion, so imaging of the chest is needed.

blocks.title: Posterior cricoarytenoid
blocks.text: The posterior cricoarytenoids are the only abductors of the vocal folds. Loss of both leaves the folds unopposed near the midline and causes airway obstruction, so bilateral injury is an emergency.

items: The oral cavity is bounded by the lips, cheeks, hard and soft palate and the floor of the mouth, and contains the tongue and teeth.
The pharynx is divided into nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx; food passes through the oropharynx and laryngopharynx.
The piriform fossae on either side of the laryngeal inlet channel food around the larynx toward the oesophagus.

points: Swallowing has a voluntary oral stage, a reflex pharyngeal stage (palatal elevation, laryngeal closure, constriction) and an oesophageal stage of peristalsis.
The larynx has nine cartilages; all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor.
Unilateral RLN injury causes a hoarse, breathy voice; bilateral injury causes stridor; the left RLN is vulnerable to thoracic lesions because it loops under the aortic arch.

questions.stem: Which stage of swallowing is under voluntary control?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: chewing and pushing the bolus back are voluntary.
distractorRationale.b: The pharyngeal stage is a reflex.
distractorRationale.c: The oesophageal stage is a reflex mediated by peristalsis.
distractorRationale.d: Only the first stage is voluntary.

questions.explanation: The oral stage involves chewing and tongue movements that are consciously controlled. Once the bolus reaches the oropharynx the pharyngeal and oesophageal stages proceed as reflexes.

questions.stem: During the pharyngeal stage, which event prevents food passing into the nasal cavity?

options.text: Elevation of the soft palate against the posterior pharyngeal wall

questions.correctOptionText: Elevation of the soft palate against the posterior pharyngeal wall

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the palate seals the nasopharynx.
distractorRationale.b: Cricopharyngeus relaxation lets food enter the oesophagus.
distractorRationale.c: The posterior cricoarytenoid opens the glottis, which would not be wanted.
distractorRationale.d: The hyoid is elevated during swallowing.

questions.explanation: The soft palate rises and contacts the posterior pharyngeal wall, closing the nasopharynx. This is accomplished by levator veli palatini and tensor veli palatini.

questions.stem: Which nerves carry the afferent limb of the swallowing reflex from the oropharynx?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: sensation from the oropharynx and pharynx travels in IX and X.
distractorRationale.b: These are motor nerves for the tongue and neck muscles.
distractorRationale.c: Motor fibres do not carry afferent signals.

questions.explanation: Afferents from the oropharynx and pharyngeal wall travel in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the medullary swallowing centre, which coordinates the motor response.

questions.stem: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is the only abductor of the vocal folds?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the arytenoids outward and opens the glottis. All other intrinsic muscles either adduct or alter tension.

questions.stem: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve rather than the recurrent laryngeal nerve?

distractorRationale.b: Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorRationale.c: Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorRationale.d: Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.explanation: The cricothyroid is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It tenses the vocal folds and its nerve is the external laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: True or false: the cricoid cartilage is the only laryngeal cartilage that forms a complete ring.
questions.explanation: The cricoid is a signet-shaped complete ring at the lower border of the larynx, whereas the thyroid cartilage is open posteriorly. This is why it offers support to the airway.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a hoarse, breathy voice immediately after a total thyroidectomy, with no breathing difficulty. Laryngoscopy shows the right vocal fold fixed near the midline. Which structure was most likely injured?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unilateral RLN injury paralyses the fold and causes hoarseness.
distractorRationale.b: External laryngeal injury causes loss of pitch range without a fixed fold.
distractorRationale.c: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue.

questions.explanation: The RLN supplies the intrinsic muscles that move the vocal fold, and lies close to the thyroid gland. Its unilateral injury leaves the fold paralysed, giving a hoarse, breathy voice but a usually adequate airway.

questions.stem: Which consequence is expected from simultaneous injury of both recurrent laryngeal nerves?

options.text: Stridor and airway obstruction from midline vocal folds
Complete loss of laryngeal sensation above the folds
Hyperabduction of the folds with a very loud voice

questions.correctOptionText: Stridor and airway obstruction from midline vocal folds

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both folds lie near the midline and the abductors are lost.
distractorRationale.c: Sensation above the folds is carried by the internal laryngeal nerve.
distractorRationale.d: Abductor function is lost, not enhanced.

questions.explanation: Bilateral RLN injury paralyses both posterior cricoarytenoids, so the folds cannot abduct and the glottis is narrowed. The result is stridor and possible airway obstruction.

questions.stem: Describe the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and explain why a left-sided thoracic lesion can cause hoarseness, whereas the right nerve is less often involved by such lesions.
markingGuide: Left RLN arises from the vagus in the thorax and loops under the aortic arch (lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum)
It ascends in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus to the larynx
Right RLN loops under the right subclavian artery near the root of the neck, a shorter intrathoracic course
Mediastinal tumours, aortic aneurysm or nodal masses can compress the left nerve
Paralysis of the vocal fold produces hoarseness and a breathy voice
questions.explanation: The left nerve has a long thoracic course around the aortic arch, so mediastinal disease commonly affects it. The right nerve passes under the subclavian artery in the root of the neck and is less often involved by such lesions.

questions.stem: Describe the pharyngeal stage of swallowing: the sequence of events, the muscles involved and the cranial nerves for afferent and efferent limbs.
markingGuide: Triggered by the bolus touching the oropharynx; afferents in IX and X
Integrated in the medullary swallowing centre
Soft palate elevated to seal the nasopharynx (levator and tensor veli palatini)
Larynx and hyoid elevated, epiglottis tilts, vocal cords adduct
Pharyngeal constrictors contract sequentially (vagus); cricopharyngeus relaxes
Efferents largely via the vagus, with IX to stylopharyngeus and V3 to tensor veli palatini
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal stage is a rapid reflex that seals the nose and airway and propels the bolus into the oesophagus. Afferents travel in IX and X, and motor output is mainly vagal.
